recommendations.text: RECOMMENDATIONS TO THE LUXEMBOURG AUTHORITIES Unless another deadline is indicated, the Luxembourg authorities are required to inform the Commission Services of the action taken or planned to address the following recommendations within 25 working days after receiving this report. It is recommended that the CA · provides detailed and comprehensive updated figures on the annual production of feeds and trade in feeds and PAP used for animal consumption, in particular trade in feeds containing processed mammalian waste. · provides detailed information on the controls carried out at farm level. 10 · ensures that traders of PAP like fishmeal used for the production of feeds are aware of the requirements of Article 2 (1) of Commission 97/735/EC and take the necessary action towards implementation. · checks for the documentation as required by Article 4 (1) of Council Directive 92/118/EEC referring to Annex I Chapter 4. during control visits to traders of petfood in those cases where the feeds are directly traded from manufacturers into Luxembourg and inform the traders about these legal requirements. · adopts instructions to ensure that carcasses and the internal organs of positive bovines are destroyed in accordance with Article 4 of Decision 97/534/EC as foreseen by Article 3 (2) of Commission Decision 98/272/EC. · focusses on sampling moribund cattle as foreseen by Commission Decision 98/272/EC rather than taking samples from slaughter cows fit for human consumption where the number of available bovines with neurological symptoms does not meet the defined target number.

NATIONAL RULES FOR SPECIFIED RISK MATERIAL Commission Decision 97/534/EC entered into force in Luxembourg as a national initiative. As no Community legislation on SRM is yet in place it is proposed that the CA ensures that the competent authority at the place of destination is informed whenever material defined as SRM is traded. This information is essential to enable the competent authority at the place of destination to apply any national rules for SRM.

RECOMMENDATION TO THE COMMISSION It is recommended to clarify whether the provisions laid down in Annex I and II to Commission Decision 97/735/EC are applicable to trade in feeds containing processed mammalian animal protein. 11

audits.title: Potato sector

recommendations.text: Correct the procedure for C.m.s. testing, so that an egg plant test is always carried out when IF tests have been positive with both antisera. (As required in Council Directive 93/85/EEC, annex I, point 5.2.11)

Correct the procedure for R. solanacearum testing, so that selective plating and/or a bio assay test is carried out routinely if an IF test is positive; - and not only if a second IF test with a different antiserum also is positive. (As required in Council Directive 98/57/EC, annex I, section I, point 2)

Consider complementing the procedure for R. solanacearum testing, so that a pathogenity test on test plants is carried out in all cases of positive IF and selective plating, (and not only if a PCR test of the pure culture is positive).

Consider measures to reduce the risk of contamination by contact at the communal packing facilities for seed potatoes. Luxembourg is requested to report to the Commission two months after receipt of the final report on action taken and/or planned on the above points. For planned action, a deadline for completion should be indicated. 14 11. audits.title: BSE

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take measures that the official veterinarians, as required by Annex I, Chapter VIII point 42 B of Council Directive 64/433/EC, record results of the ante-mortem inspections. With regard to veterinary certificate accompanying emergency slaughtered animals:

The competent authority should take measures to ensure that requirements as laid down in Article 6 (e) of the Council Directive 64/433/EC are met. 26 With regard to the approval procedures of the premises slaughtering on the farm:
The competent authority should take measures to ensure that the conditions laid down in Article 4 of the Council Directive 64/433/EEC are met. With regard to the feed ban:
The competent authority should enforce controls on the feed mills, in the intermediaries and at the farm level as already recommended in the previous report DG (XXIV/1506/1998).

The competent authority should include risk assessment in targeting official feed samples for the possible presence of bone fragments in compound feed and take measures to comply with the requirements for labelling of final samples as laid down in Commission Directive 76/371/EEC.

The competent authority should ensure appropriate corrective actions in cases of MMBM contamination. The time delay associated with laboratory results should be reduced or some other solution provided. With regard to epidemio-surveillance of BSE:
The competent authority should produce clear guidelines for the destruction of BSE contaminated carcasses and internal organs as already recommended in the previous report DG (XXIV/1506/1998).

The competent authority should ensure that information is collected on each sampled bovine, as regards the clinical history, signs and age of the animal in addition to the service, which has requested sampling. This information should be available to the Commission Services on request.
The competent authority should fulfil all requirements as regards the contents of the annual report as laid down in Annex II of 98/272/EC, as amended. With regard to SRM:

The competent authority should set up a system to ensure and check that SRM is removed and destroyed in accordance with Annex I, points 2 to 5 of Commission Decision 2000/418/EC. In addition to this, the competent authority should guarantee that requirements for sending SRM to other Member States for incineration under conditions as laid down in Article 4(2) of Commission Decision 97/735/EC are met.

The competent authority should ensure adequate separation between SRM and other animal waste at all times in slaughterhouses and enforce measures to avoid cross-contamination during the removal of SRM. 27
The competent authority should take measures to ensure that the official controls on the ban on pithing are effective. With regard to animal identification and registration:
The competent authority should improve the selection of holdings to be inspected taking into account the results of previous CII checks and communication of the data to the competent authority.
The competent authority should carry out controls on all animals present on a holding during a cattle identification inspection.
The competent authority should take measures to reduce the number of delayed notifications. With regard to the treatment of wastewater in the collection centre:

The competent authority should take measures to prevent spreading of pathogens with untreated wastewater. 28 9. audits.title: Use of plant protection products and residues in foodstuffs

recommendations.text: The competent authorities of Luxembourg should establish clear inspection procedures, including infringement procedures, for controls of the marketing and use of plant protection products. These controls should include check of information appearing on the label, sampling and formulation analysis.

The competent authorities of Luxembourg should ensure that the results of controls on the marketing and use of plant protection products are reported to 14 the Member States and the Commission in compliance with article 17 of Directive 91/414/EEC.
The competent authorities of Luxembourg should transpose the Council Directive 93/99/EEC in national legislation and inform the Commission thereof in compliance with article 9 of this Directive.

The competent authorities of Luxembourg should ensure that processed food is monitored for pesticide residues and that the sampling of fruit and vegetable follows accurately Commission Directive 79/700/EEC.

The competent authorities of Luxembourg should ensure that infringements regarding pesticide residues are clearly defined and that the actions which are taken in the event of infringements are appropriate and include communication with other concerned services.

The competent authorities of Luxembourg should make effort to speed up accreditation of the laboratory carrying out pesticide residue analysis. The implementation of the EU quality control procedures should be supported by appropriate resources.

The competent authorities of Luxembourg should designate a body responsible for the assessment of the official laboratories. An action plan in response to the recommendations of chapter 7.1, points (1), (2), (3), (4), (5), (6) and (7) should be forwarded to the Commission Services within 2 months after the dispatch of the final report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the Competent Authority will address each recommendation. 7.2. To the Commission Services The Commission Services should consider taking action against Luxembourg for the non-transposition of the Council Directive 93/99/EEC.

recommendations.text: Take immediate action to implement the appropriate measures in the two establishments where particularly serious shortcomings were identified, in order to eliminate the risks to the safety of food products placed on the market by these establishments.

audits.title: Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies

recommendations.text: The Central Competent Authority should bring the national provisions in-line with EC Regulation 999/2001, in particular Article 13 (1) (b) (the inquiry of animals at risk).
The Central Competent Authority should increase efforts already made to improve the TSE passive surveillance and measures following confirmation of the presence of TSE.
The Central Competent Authority should request the NRL to organise a ring test for the two approved laboratories

The Central Competent Authority should evaluate data collected at various levels of supervision in order to monitor the epidemio-surveillance programme for BSE and Scrapie. All eligible bovine fallen stock should be sampled and tested.

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that progeny, parents and cohort animals of confirmed TSE cases can be traced. 8.2. WITH REGARD TO BOVINE IDENTIFICATION AND REGISTRATION: 1. The CA should properly address up the recommendations set out in the previous report, and in particular: i. the selection of holdings to be inspected should take into account the results of previous CII checks and communication to the CA; ii. controls should be carried out on all animals present on a holding during a cattle identification inspection; 24 iii. slaughterhouses and the collection centre should notify without delay the animals slaughtered/fallen to the database. 8.3. WITH REGARD TO THE FEED BAN: 1. The CA should not tolerate any presence of prohibited PAP in feeding stuffs and corrective actions should be taken promptly also for low level of contamination. 2. The CA should ensure a risk-based approach in the feed ban control. Sampling should be targeted at materials, times and places, where the probability of finding forbidden substances (MBM and unlicensed fishmeal) is higher. 3. The CA should identify means to keep the time necessary to deliver the results of the feed tests as short as possible. 4. The CA should intensify the control of mobile mixer and home compounder and put in place specific requirement for these premises ensuring that the total feed ban is applied. 8.4. WITH REGARD TO SRM: 1. The CA should ensure proper and prompt feed back information from the collection centre to the plants in order that an effective reconciliation between SRM produced and destroyed can be carried out. 2. The CA should review the dispatch of ANIMO messages to ensure that the competent authority in the country of destination is able to perform timely controls. 8.5. WITH REGARD TO FARMS APPROVED TO SLAUGHTER ANIMALS : The CA should confirm that the legal requirements for the approval of farms slaughtering animals are in compliance with Article 4 of the Council Directive 64/433/EEC. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/8568/2002 The competent authorities from Luxembourg informed the FVO in their response to the draft report on actions already taken or planned to be taken: With regard to TSE controls in bovine, ovine and caprine animals 1) That corrective measures drawn up in gathering information regard of tested animals should result in future in a coherent number of tests carried out. 2) That from 1 September 2002, the rendering centre operator is introducing an additional lorry equipped with a system for separate loading of carcasses to be submitted to the rapid detection tests, it is making technically possible to carry out BSE tests on all eligible carcasses. 3) That an information and awareness campaign to be organised during the winter season should improve awareness and knowledge among the various players with regard to scrapie in sheep 25 4) That more consistent monitoring and testing of animals exposed to the same, possibly contaminated, feedingstuffs is planned. 5) That a revision of the Scenario will enable this to become a contingency plan.
That contacts have been established with the reference laboratory in Belgium to organise periodic comparative test with laboratories located in Luxembourg. With regard to the feed ban
In the event of consumption of potentially contaminated feedingstuffs, animals likely to have consumed this feedingstuff will be tested at an earlier age.

When feed from neighbouring Member States is noted cross-contaminated with PAP the Authorities from Luxembourg will inform the CCA in the countries concerned, even at a very low level of contamination (i.e. less than 1). With regard to SRM

New instructions concerning controls of SRM, and the documentation of those controls, will be set out in a specific circular. Improvements in the procedure for the conciliation of SRM are planned, in close co-operation between the Veterinary Services Administration and the operator of the waste collection centre.
The ANIMO notification will be speeded up. With regard to farms approved to slaughter animals
That the Community legislation proposal on food hygiene and specific hygiene rules applicable to foodstuffs of animal origin should enable the competent authority to deal with this problem. 26

audits.title: Pesticides

recommendations.text: The competent authority should transpose amendments of Directive 91/414/EEC into national law without delay.

In accordance with Article 17 of Directive 91/414/EEC, the competent authorities should introduce comprehensive inspection procedures for controlling the marketing of plant protection products, including planning, performance, reporting and follow-up, and train inspectors for the implementation of these controls. Comprehensive controls of users of plant protection products should be extended to cover all users. 17
The competent authority should ensure that complete reports of the control activities on marketing and use are sent to the Commission in accordance with Article 17 of Directive 91/414/EEC.
The competent authority should ensure that sampling is carried out fully in accordance with Commission Directive 2002/63/EC.

The competent authority should ensure that analytical results from pesticide residue data are sufficiently supported by quality control procedures, in accordance with Article 4 of Regulation 645/2002 and Guidance Document SANCO/10476/2003.

The competent authority should increase the range of pesticides and metabolites in the analytical screens, so as to better reflect those substances being marketed and to ensure adequate enforcement of pesticide MRLs as specified in Directives 76/895/EEC, 86/362/EEC and 90/642/EEC.

The competent authorities should ensure that analytical methods with the required sensitivity are used to enforce MRLs specified by Commission Directives 91/321/EEC and 96/5/EC. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. With regard to recommendation (1), the competent authorities stated that the amendments to Directive 91/414/EEC have now been transposed up to 2006. With regard to recommendation (2), the Customs provided an action plan with details regarding training of inspectors, and regarding planning, performance and reporting of controls. With regard to recommendation (4), the competent authorities provided an action plan in order to fully comply with Directive 2002/63/EC.

citations.text: In addition to the responsibilities stated under paragraph 7, ASTA is the CA in charge of decision making with regard to compliance or non-compliance of pesticide wholesalers, as part of official controls on the marketing of PPPs. ASTA staff are also responsible for carrying out of ad-hoc inspections at small scale growers and landscapers (see paragraphs 36 and 74 below). ASTA stated, however, that their staff do not have the status of "judicial police officers" ("officier de police judiciaire" (OPJ)). In order for ASTA staff to take any of the measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, they have to be accompanied by police officers. Once the Regulation, listed under paragraph 2, has been adopted, ASTA staff will have the OPJ status allowing them to take enforcement measures in the case of irregularities identified. This is not fully in line with the requirements of Article 4 (2) (e) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Official controls on both marketing and use of PPPs are performed in accordance with written instruction, in a uniform manner, which ensures consistency and operation of PPP wholesalers and professional users to the same standards. However, the complications for ASTA staff to take enforcement measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in the case of irregularities identified at pesticide distributors, small scale growers and landscapers could compromise the effectiveness of official controls. 5.3. ASTA staff do not have the OPJ status allowing them to take enforcement measures (see paragraph 8 above), unless accompanied by police officers. However, there are provisions in the PPPA, allowing the Minister of Agriculture to take a number of administrative measures, which correspond to some of these, laid down in Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. According to information provided during the audit, in the case of irregularities identified and reported by ADA, ASTA staff could only recommend non- compliant operators as to what corrective measures to take in order to remedy the situation. There are no other follow-up actions by any of the CAs in order to verify that adequate action has been taken, as required by Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

According to information provided by ASTA, at the time of the audit, national legal provisions and rules regarding penalties applicable to infringements of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Directive 128/2009/EC were laid down in the PPPA. For the same reasons, as listed above (see paragraphs 8 and 70), ASTA staff are not allowed to impose penalties. At the time of the audit, imposition of penalties, as well as any further measures in the case of serious infringements, were the responsibility of the Court of Justice. Once the Regulation, listed under paragraph 2, has been adopted, ASTA staff will have the powers to enforce the imposition of the penalties referred to in the final bullet points of paragraphs 2 and 3. Controls on the use of PPPs

At grower level, in the case of ad-hoc inspections by ASTA, the situation with regard to enforcement measures is similar to that described under paragraph 70 above. The reason is the same; ASTA staff do not have the OPJ status to apply any of the measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, or to impose sanctions. Conclusions on Enforcement Measures

For official controls on the use of PPPs, a system is in place for decision making on compliance with national and EU legal requirements, including enforcement measures and sanctions. However, this is not the case for official controls on the marketing of PPPs and for professional users with no extensive use of PPPs (landscapers and small scale growers), where there is a risk that non-compliances are not remedied by infringing operators, as no corrective measures are recommended to non-compliant operators and due to the absence of verification by any of the CAs. The complications with regard to imposition of penalties is one further complication. As a result of all these, the effectiveness of official controls at the operators concerned could be compromised. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION In Luxembourg, well-established systems are in place for official controls on the marketing and use of PPPs. Inspections are risk based and well targeted, in particular, with regard to their timing. Traceability and documentary checks at PPP wholesalers, including mass balance, as seen to be performed are considered a strong point. A very similar approach to PPP marketing controls was applied at user level. However, there has been a significant delay in the transposition of certain EU requirements on the sustainable use of pesticides. As a result, there is a risk that not all operators work to the same standards and in such a way so as to avoid unnecessary risk to human health and the environment. In addition, shortcomings were identified with regard to labelling checks. Shortcomings identified with regard to enforcement measures at PPP wholesalers, landscapers and small scale growers, can weaken the effectiveness of official controls. 7. recommendations.text: To put arrangements in place to ensure that documentary checks of veterinary certificates and documentation on animal welfare of live animals are implemented correctly in line with the requirements of Annex I to Commission Decision 97/794/EC and Article 21(2) of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion 34. Associated findings: 5 and 14.

citations.text: Detailed documented procedures are in place to carry out the official controls and take samples correctly for live animals, products of animal origin and non-animal origin. The audit team noted one exception regarding the instruction for the controls of live animals, which does not require a check of the route plan for animals going on to travel long distances to ensure that proper resting times have been scheduled in order to respect animal welfare requirements during transportation (see findings 14 and 32). Conclusion on the organisation of the competent authorities and of official controls

The audit team noted several shortcomings in relation to the documentary checks of live animals: Several consignments of live animals were accepted when certificates did not comply with the detailed rules for documentary checks for live animals laid down in Annex I to Commission Decision 97/794/EC. In particular, several non- conformities were noted where the veterinary certificates were accepted without evidence that the certificate consisted of a single sheet or two or more pages that were part of a single and indivisible sheet of paper containing a sequence of numbered pages. The BIP staff accepted the route plans for breeding pigs which did not reflect the distance and resting times required during the long onward transportation to their destination in other EU Member States. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 21(2) of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. The national instruction for the controls of live animals does not require staff to check the route plan for animals going on to travel long distances to ensure that proper resting times have been scheduled (see finding 5). Since Luxembourg BIP is one of the most important entries into the EU for breeding pigs (to Croatia, Czech Republic, France, Spain), this shortcoming significantly impacts animal welfare requirements during transportation. The CVEDA was incorrectly filled in in cases when dead/missing animals were detected during the identity and physical checks at the BIP, contrary to the requirements of Annex II of Commission Regulation (EC) No 282/2004.

The veterinary checks at the BIP are mostly carried out correctly and the decisions taken on the consignments are generally appropriate to satisfy the import control requirements. In some cases of live animals, BIP staff accepted consignments with inappropriate veterinary certificates and documentation related to the animal welfare of live animals which might lead to non-compliant consignments of live animals being accepted or animal welfare requirements not being respected.

citations.text: A recently developed procedure has been adopted to determine the main risk associated with each official control system, which identifies certain areas of the food chain (e.g. production, processing, transport etc.) where controls are carried out. This approach to risk-based planning is a starting point but does not reflect the diversity of official controls and sectoral requirements within each of the 21 official control areas. As the broader official control areas have not been subject to a more detailed breakdown, the risks relating to the different aspects have not been explicitly identified (e.g. product, process, establishment type etc.). Furthermore, there is no methodology in place to assign a risk ranking to each aspect. For example, in the case of food hygiene, OSQCA did not break this area down into official controls in different types of establishment (mobile food sellers, restaurants, primary production, processing plants, wholesalers, retailers, mass catering etc.), size of establishment/volume of production, production processes etc. OSQCA recognised that it would be useful to carry out more in-depth audits that cover sector-specific requirements based on risk but this is not possible given the current very limited resources and lack of access to technical experts. 12

The strategy for the current three-year cycle is to audit each control system at least once to gain an overview of the state of play of official controls. This means effectively that risk prioritisation is limited to the order in which the official control areas will be audited. The concept of 'adequate coverage of all relevant areas of activity' of point 5.1 of Decision 2006/677/EC was taken to mean 'audit' of all relevant areas, rather than risk- based consideration of all relevant areas. OSQCA stated that this would be considered for the next audit cycle and that it would also reflect on lengthening the audit cycle to five years to facilitate more in-depth audits.

Whilst OSQCA did not carry out audits for several years, it is now on track to audit the horizontal aspects of all 21 official control areas in the 2017-2019 cycle. However, given the scarce resources, the scope and depth of these audits is limited to evaluating compliance with the horizontal requirements of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

A procedure for determining the risks associated with each official control system has been recently developed but is not sufficiently detailed to identify risk-based priorities, nor does the planning cover the actual performance of official controls and diversity of sectoral requirements. The impact on the current audit cycle is limited, however, given that a) OSQCA's aim is to gain a quick overview of all official control systems after a long period without audits, and b) there are currently only resources available to audit horizontal requirements. 5.2.5 Implementation of the audit process 5.2.5.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that "Audit" "means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." In section 5.1 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on the `Systematic Approach', including: "A systematic approach should be applied to the planning, conduct, follow-up and management of audits. To that end, the audit process should: 13 ....... -- be supported by documented audit procedures and records to ensure consistency between auditors and to demonstrate that a systematic approach is followed, -- include procedures for generating audit findings, including the identification of evidence of compliance and noncompliance, as appropriate, and for preparing, approving and distributing audit reports, -- include procedures to review audit conclusions, in order to identify system-wide strengths and weaknesses in the control system, disseminate best practice and ensure the monitoring of corrective and preventive actions, -- be monitored and reviewed to ensure the audit programme's objectives have been met and to identify opportunities for improvement." Section 6.1 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on implementation of the Audit Process: "To comply with the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the audit system should cover the following three points set out in Article 2(6): (a) Verification of compliance with planned arrangements in order to provide assurances that official controls are carried out as intended and that any instructions or guidelines given to staff carrying out the controls are followed. This may largely be addressed by document review, but will also require on-site verification. The audit team will require good generic audit knowledge and skills to address this audit objective. (b) Verification of the effective implementation of planned arrangements. In order to assess effectiveness, that is the extent to which planned results are achieved, on-site operational implementation must be included. This should include an assessment of the quality and consistency of the controls and should involve on-site audit activities. citations.text: The audit team noted that in 2019 nearly 45% of agricultural land was in water protection zones participating in agri-environment schemes, with nearly two years remaining in which to achieve the aim to have 70% of land under these schemes as set out in the current NAP. Nonetheless, the action to develop a tool for advisors to help identify risks of water contamination was discontinued because of staffing issues. Moreover, while a 10 m buffer zone along SW, where the use of PPP is prohibited, came into force in 2018 through national legislation, this provision is not yet enforced during official controls.

With regard to prohibiting or restricting the use of certain PPPs in water protection zones, the CA has identified AS of particular concern, and has established risk mitigation measures for their use. The use of PPPs containing S-metolachlor is prohibited in Luxembourg, and the use of PPPs containing metazachlor is allowed only outside water protection zones. Nonetheless, PPPs containing these AS, are still authorised for placing on the market in Luxembourg. Representatives from the SPV explained that this measure took into account the fact that some Luxembourgish farmers are interested to buy the afore-mentioned PPPs in Luxembourg to use on land, which they own in neighbouring countries, where these PPPs are authorised for use. The audit team noted that the afore- mentioned measures have been in place since the adoption of Grand Ducal Regulation of 12 April 2015, and the results of the water monitoring in 2019 and 2020 show some good results with regard to the presence of the substances metazachlor and S- 18 metolachlor/metolachlor. Nonetheless, due to the still significant presence of their main metabolites (metazachlor-ESA and metolachlor-ESA) both in SW and GW, the effectiveness of these measures is still limited (see findings 59 and 63).

GW analytical results for 2019 show that, of the 489 samples taken, there were 312 exceedances3. Exceedances for metazachlor-ESA (a metazachlor metabolite) were found in 149 samples (30% of the samples) and for S-metolachlor-ESA in 110 samples (22% of the samples), whereas 23 samples (5% of total samples) saw exceedances for the sum of all PPPs. Results from 2020 show that, of the 355 samples taken, there were 223 exceedances3. Exceedances for metazachlor-ESA were found in 90 samples (25% of the samples) and for S-metolachlor-ESA (a metolochlor metabolite) in 68 samples (19% of the samples). Exceedances for the sum of all PPPs were found in 28 samples (8% of the samples).

SW analytical results for 2019 show that, of the 602 samples taken, there were 43 analyses in which AS were detected at levels exceeding the respective environmental quality standard, and 776 analyses in which AS exceeded the DW regulatory standard of 0.1µg/l. Results from 2020 show that, of the 700 samples taken, AS levels exceeding the respective environmental quality standard were detected in 71 analyses and the DW regulatory standard of 0.1µg/l was exceeded in 767 of the analyses. For both years, the DW limit breaches were largely accounted for by detections of metazachlor-ESA (36% of samples in 2019 and 20% in 2020) and S-metolachlor-ESA (5% of samples in 2019 and 9% in 2020), glyphosate (11% of samples in 2019 and 9% in 2020) and its metabolite AMPA (41% of samples in 2019 and 42% in 2020). The CA indicated that the majority of samples analysed have some level of contamination present.

In the monitoring programme of 2019, 192 samples were analysed with 15 of them found to exceed the DW regulatory limit. In 2020, 150 samples were taken, and the DW regulatory limit was exceeded in nine samples. The contamination in both years was caused in all cases except one, by the metabolites of metazachlor and S-metolachlor. Conclusions on water protection

The NAP includes a number of measures to protect water bodies from the impact of PPPs. Some of them have been put in place by the CAs, or are in progress, in particular the ban on the use of certain substances of particular concern and the increase of agricultural land, subject to agri-environment schemes in water protection zones. Others have been discontinued, or are not enforced yet as is the case for the 10 m buffer zone to protect SW. recommendations.text: To ensure that the FBO's food safety management system and procedures guarantee to the extent possible, that fresh meat does not bear any visible faecal contamination when presented for PMI and that the FBO take appropriate and timely corrective action when contamination is detected on the carcases, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Recommendation based on conclusion No 70. Associated finding Nos 41, 54, 57 and 58.

citations.text: FBO staff regularly presented carcases with visible contamination for PMI, which created extra work for the vacataires, some of which were busy removing the contamination during PMI.

The audit team did not observe, in any of the two establishments, any FBO staff checking on carcase contamination and taking suitable corrective action (i.e. immediately removing all visible contamination, before presenting those carcases for PMI). The official staff had taken up the task of removing the contamination before declaring the carcases fit for human consumption. HACCP Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Findings

The FBOs food safety management systems checked by the audit team included sufficient controls on animal identification, FCI and on the cleanliness and the state of health of the livestock. In relation to carcase monitoring for the presence of contamination, the FBOs had decided to set a frequency of two checks per week.

The CA accepted this frequency of controls over FBO monitoring of carcass contamination as sufficient. At the time of the visits, especially during cattle production, the OVs and vacataires were seen to be busy removing visible faecal contamination from 9 a significant number of carcases. No monitoring by the FBO on the carcases presented for PMI was observed, nor any action to avoid or to eliminate the contamination on those carcases. Microbiological criteria Legal requirements Articles 35 and 36 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

The shortcomings identified in how the OVs deal with contamination on carcases, with lack of enforcement to ensure that FBOs monitor the hygiene of operations and take suitable and timely action before carcases are presented for PMI with visible contamination.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the CCA has documented procedures in place, containing instructions for staff performing official controls, to ensure the effectiveness, appropriateness, quality and consistency of those controls and other official activities at slaughterhouse level, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 28. Associated finding Nos 11, 24, 51, 52, 53 and 61.

citations.text: There are several official checklists that the CCA have created and are used during the day-to-day activities at the establishments and also during yearly audits. The daily checklist includes pre-operational checks and animal welfare checks. There are no checklists, nor documented procedures in place for other official controls, including operational hygiene related activities. For those cases, the system relies on verbal instructions and guidance and support from central office staff.

Occasionally different officers gave very different deadlines to similar non-compliances. This was evident when comparing several yearly audit reports. As explained by the CA, this has improved as a result to recent changes in the official controls team, with the current team providing more realistic and suitable enforcement.
The lack of documented procedures or guidance affects the effectiveness of delivery of official controls and results in some controls not fully carried out or not carried out in a consistent manner.

Despite these daily checks, in some instances, the OVs didn't manage to identify some problems concerning lack of cleanliness that were later identified during the yearly audit carried out by central office staff.
There are no dedicated checklists or written guidance to aid the OVs when monitoring the hygiene standards during the slaughter operation.
In relation to the operational hygiene requirements, the OV controls did not identify a number of generalised and recurrent unhygienic practices (see p.20) which were observed during the audit.

According to the records checked and discussions with CA staff, the establishment OVs had not identified any problems in relation to FBO's own sampling. However, the audit team found that the sampling programmes were not fully in line with legislation. Issues including the fact that FBOs do not take the samples randomly during production but tend to sample batches or the use of alternative sampling arrangements without demonstration of equivalence (i.e. chicken tested before chilling or beef tested during chilling).

recommendations.text: To ensure that in slaughterhouses that make use of the derogation on the timing of post-mortem inspection, sufficient measures are taken so inspection of the carcases and offal can be performed as required, in accordance with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Recommendation based on conclusion No 71.

citations.text: The post-mortem inspection arrangements in the slaughterhouse that makes use of the time of inspection derogation is not in line with EU law which requires correlation of carcases and offal irrespective of the delay in PMI. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The organisation and structure of the CA and its control system provide a largely adequate framework for the delivery of official controls, which are delivered at the established frequency and generally cover the relevant aspects. Some systemic weaknesses have, however, an impact on their effectiveness: The current legal instrument does not provide the possibility to impose fines. This is a longstanding issue, already identified in previous DG (SANTE) audits, that limits the efficiency of official controls, in particular when FBOs do not resolve non-compliances by the deadlines imposed by the CA. The CA explained that a solution to this has been in preparation for a number of years and that a draft bill was currently being studied. The guidance and procedures available to official veterinarians are limited in some areas, which does not ensure that all the appropriate points are supervised and result in problems of 11 consistency of controls. The supervision and identification of training needs are not adequate and, as a result, some official veterinarians were not able to identify certain operational hygiene non-compliances, nor enforce their correction. The PMI arrangements in the slaughterhouse that makes use of the time of inspection derogation do not ensure full correlation of carcases and offal, as offal are not saved and presented for inspection. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held in Luxembourg on 12 May 2023 with the CCA. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit and advised the CCA of the relevant time limits for the production of the report and their response.
